title: NHS Clears Five AI Tools to Help Spot Prostate Cancer on MRI Scans
excerpt: NICE has recommended five AI programs for NHS use over a two-year evidence-gathering period. They highlight possible cancer on prostate MRI scans for radiologists — who still review every scan — but NICE says proof of accuracy in routine practice is still limited.
body:
• NICE has recommended five AI tools — AI-Rad Companion Prostate MR, DeepHealth Prostate, ProstatID, Prostate Intelligence (Pi) and QP-Prostate — for NHS use during a two-year evidence-generation period.
  • The software highlights areas on a prostate MRI where cancer might be present; a radiologist still reviews every scan and every AI result before any care decision.
  • There is no single proven accuracy figure yet: NICE says the evidence is limited and inconsistent across studies, which is why use is conditional on collecting real-world NHS data on accuracy, biopsies and outcomes.
  • The scale of the problem is absolute, not relative: more than 58,000 men were diagnosed with prostate cancer in England in 2023, and demand for pre-biopsy MRI scans is rising.

NHS doctors in England are to use artificial intelligence to help diagnose prostate cancer, after the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommended five AI tools in draft guidance. The programs are designed to highlight areas on a prostate MRI scan where cancer might be present, making it easier for radiologists to spot and report, NICE said.

The five technologies — AI-Rad Companion Prostate MR, DeepHealth Prostate, ProstatID, Prostate Intelligence (Pi) and QP-Prostate — can be used in the NHS as options for two years while further evidence is generated. Two others, hProstate and mdProstate, were not recommended for NHS funding because no clinical or cost-effectiveness evidence was available for them.

"These AI technologies have the potential to act like a second pair of eyes, helping radiologists review prostate MRI scans. They have the potential to make MRI reporting more accurate and could help identify people whose scans need priority review."

— Dr Anastasia Chalkidou, Programme Director for HealthTech, NICE

How the tools work — and what they do not do

The AI can identify and outline possible areas of cancer on an MRI scan, classify risk and produce information to support the radiologist interpreting it. It does not diagnose on its own. "They would support, not replace, radiologists, who would still review the scan and the AI results before any decisions about patient care," said Dr Adrian Hayter, a GP and chief medical officer at NICE, in coverage by Pulse Today. Professor Peter Johnson, NHS national clinical director for cancer, made the same point: a radiologist will review every scan.

https://x.com/Telegraph/status/2113513322066649487

MRI matters because not every prostate tumour needs treatment. Some can be monitored safely, since they are unlikely to cause symptoms. A good MRI read helps clinicians decide who needs a biopsy or further tests to confirm cancer that does need treatment — and, if the AI performs as hoped, who can be spared an unnecessary biopsy.

The honest accuracy picture

Readers should treat headline claims about AI accuracy with care. NICE's independent committee concluded the tools have the potential to improve the accuracy and consistency of MRI interpretation, particularly in settings without specialist expertise — but it also found the available evidence limited, with findings not always consistent across studies. NICE has published no single sensitivity or accuracy percentage for these tools, and any claim that they are a proven percentage more accurate would go beyond the evidence. What the NHS will now measure over two years is concrete: diagnostic accuracy in routine practice, the number of biopsies, waiting times for biopsy and diagnosis, radiologist capacity and workflow, costs, patient outcomes, and performance across different groups of patients.

The need is measurable. There were more than 58,000 new diagnoses of prostate cancer in England in 2023, and prostate cancer is the most common cancer in England. Demand for prostate MRI has increased because pre-biopsy scans are now routinely used to confirm or rule out disease, adding pressure to radiology teams already stretched by workforce shortages.

What this means for patients

For a man referred for a prostate MRI in England, the practical change is that an AI program may pre-read his scan and flag areas of concern for the radiologist, with the aim of a faster, more consistent report and quicker answers. Health Innovation Minister James Frith called it "smart, safe adoption of AI" that supports rather than replaces clinicians. The draft guidance is now open for consultation before final guidance is published, and the tools' NHS future will depend on the evidence the next two years produce. For UK readers of Indian origin — a community heavily represented among NHS doctors and patients alike — the rollout is one to watch in their own local trusts as adoption begins.
